claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is modeled as a disordered FCC solid solution.
Dislocations nucleate primarily at free surfaces in FeNiCrMn.
Pre-existing vacancy clusters are primary dislocation-nucleation sites in FeNiCrMn.
Local stress concentrations at surfaces or vacancy clusters trigger nucleation when they exceed the CRSS for Shockley-partial emission.
The deformation carriers are 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations on {111} planes.
Glide of Shockley partials creates intrinsic stacking faults.
The HCP-like regions are single-layer intrinsic stacking faults embedded in the FCC lattice.
The HCP-like regions lack the long-range periodicity and thermodynamic stability of a true HCP phase.
Dislocation nucleation is driven by thermal activation and defect-induced stress concentration.
High strain rates prevent dislocation annihilation and consequently increase dislocation density.
Yield-strength insensitivity to strain rate is caused by dominance of the Peierls barrier for FCC partial dislocations.
The Peierls-barrier mechanism for FCC partials is less strain-rate-sensitive than the BCC double-kink mechanism.
Loading along <11-1> aligns a {111} slip-plane normal with the loading axis and maximizes resolved shear stress.
<110> loading gives lower Schmid factors for the dominant partial-dislocation modes than <11-1> loading.
The maximum yield stress is higher for <110> loading than for <11-1> loading.
Dislocation nucleation produces a sharp stress drop followed by a plateau or gradual hardening associated with stacking-fault formation.
No twinning occurs during the modeled deformation.
No true HCP phase transformation occurs during the modeled deformation.
Yield strength decreases as temperature increases.
Yield-strength strain-rate sensitivity is negligible from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The orientation argument says that aligning the loading axis with a slip-plane normal maximizes resolved shear on that plane. Loading normal to a specified slip plane instead gives zero resolved shear on that plane, so the stated geometry and claimed Schmid-factor consequence are internally incompatible.

The predicted post-yield response is a plateau or gradual hardening due to intrinsic stacking faults, whereas the falsification rule characterizes intrinsic-stacking-fault behavior as continuous softening. These incompatible descriptions make the proposed stress-response discriminator ambiguous.
